common_name: Encore Mandarin (Very Late-Season UC Riverside Mandarin)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root citrus in spring after frost danger has passed, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Encore ripens even later than Gold Nugget, often holding on the tree into spring.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures. Encore, released by the University of California Riverside citrus breeding program, is prized above all for ripening extremely late, holding excellent eating quality on the tree well into spring at a point when nearly every other mandarin variety has finished, giving growers fresh mandarins for months longer than a standard planting would otherwise allow. The rich, deeply flavored, sweet-tart fruit contains noticeable seeds, unlike many modern seedless mandarins, but the flavor intensity and remarkably extended season have made it a favorite among citrus collectors and home growers who value variety over convenience. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection

common_name: Lee Mandarin (Clementine x Orlando Tangelo Cross)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root citrus in spring after frost danger has passed, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures. Lee was bred by USDA researchers in Florida from a cross of Clementine mandarin and Orlando tangelo, producing medium-sized, deep orange fruit with a rich, sweet, aromatic flavor that ripens in early to midseason, making it a useful bridge variety between the earliest and latest mandarins in a mixed home citrus planting. The tree is productive and the fruit easy to peel, with the fine, tender segments typical of good mandarin breeding, and while it contains some seeds it remains popular among Florida and Gulf Coast home growers for its outstanding eating quality. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize regularly with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root citrus in spring after frost danger has passed, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Fallglo ripens notably early, often ready by early fall, giving its name.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures. Fallglo was bred by USDA researchers in Florida from a cross involving Bower citrus and Temple orange, producing large, deep orange, easy-peeling fruit with rich, sweet flavor that ripens notably early in the citrus season, often ready to harvest by early fall well ahead of most other mandarins — the trait that gives the variety its name. The tree is vigorous and productive, and the early ripening window makes Fallglo a good choice for growers wanting to open their mandarin harvest as soon as possible each year. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit size and quality.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root citrus in spring after frost danger has passed, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; satsumas are among the most cold-hardy true citrus, tolerating brief drops into the low 20s°F once established, making Miyagawa a strong fit for Gulf Coast zone 9.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, choosing a warm, sheltered site since even cold-hardy satsumas benefit from added winter protection at the northern edge of their range. Miyagawa is one of the oldest and most widely propagated satsuma strains, a Japanese selection prized for consistently early ripening, seedless fruit with the loose, easy-peeling skin and sweet, low-acid, nearly seedless flesh that makes satsumas so popular for fresh eating and for introducing children to citrus. The compact, naturally dwarfing tree bears young and heavily, and its combination of good cold tolerance and dependable early production has made it one of the standard satsuma selections offered by Gulf Coast citrus nurseries. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit quality.
